full_judgment:
5. A person would be necessary party in a suit if he ought to have been jointed, that is to say, in whose absence no effective decree can be passed at all. He would be a proper party to be impleaded if his presence is necessary for effectual or complete adjudication. Now, it is true that in a suit for specific performance the general rule is that a stranger to the contract cannot be sued upon it. Only the parties to the contract are, according to that rule, necessary and sufficient parties. Hut the general rule is subject to certain modifications. For instance, strangers are made parties as an exception to the rule in cases of novation; and in cases where it is desirable to avoid multiplicity of suits as contemplated by Order 1, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 7. Mr. Ansar Ali has next referred to the case of Muhammad Ishaq vs. Mst. Jamila Begum and others reported in P.L.D. 1955 (Lahore) 644 wherein it has been held that where the title of the vendor it at issue it may be necessary to allow parties outside the contract to be added for effective and complete adjudication of the matter. In that case it was urged before the High Court in justification of impleading defendant Nos. 2 and 3 that unless they were impleaded the question of title of defendant No. 1 could not be effectively adjudicated upon. Kaikaus J. sitting single while upholding the contention observed thus: "There is no doubt that generally in suits for specific performance only the parties to the contract or those against whom the contract can to any extent be enforced should be impleaded as defendants. That is the ordinary rule but it is subject to exceptions and does not debar the impleading of a person claiming an interest adversely to the vendor and the vendee when the circumstances of a case so require. If in the present case there be no adjudication with respect to the ownership of the property in dispute between defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 2 the plaintiff, though he gets a decree in the present suit, may be deprived of it in litigation with defendants Nos. 2 and 3 and thus may be forced to file another suit for compensation against defendant No. 1. It may be said that defendant Nos. 2 and 3 are not necessary parties to the suit for the definition of necessary party is that without his getting impleaded no effective decreein the suit at all. It is not necessary for me to decide that question. There can be no doubt however, that unless and until defendants Nos. 2 and 3 are joined in the suit, the matters in dispute between the parties to this litigation cannot be effectively and completely adjudicated upon. To exclude defendants No 2 and 3 from this Suit may result in causing loss to the plaintiff and may also lead to multiplicity of suits." 

 8. In the case of Mir Hashmat Ali Vs. Birendra Kumar Ghosh and others reported in (1964) 16 DLR 239 = PLD 1965 (Dacca) 56 Murshed J, sitting in a Division Bench seems to have gone further in holding that specific performance will be granted or refused on considerations of equity and not merely on the terms of the contract and the Court under such circumstances has a wider discretion to add to the suit a party who will be able to place before it, facts and circumstances relevant to the suit upon which the Court may refuse to enforce the contract. Mr. Ansar Ali has also cited; decision of the then Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Sh. Barkatullah and another Vs. Khawaja Mohammad Ibrahim reported in (1970) 22 DLR (SC) 419= P.L.D. 1970 S.C. 483 wherein a subsequent lessee has been held to be a necessary party to plaintiff's suit for specific performance of agreement contained in a compromise deed. It has been held in that case "as a general rule the second lessee cannot be sued upon the contract to which he was not a party i.e. no decree for possession can be passed against him. The suit for specific performance would therefore fail though a decree for damages may be passed against the lessor for breach of contract However, if the second lessee is in possession and has notice of the contract on which the suit is based, he could then be sued upon and a decree for possession passed against him." 

 9. In the instant case the petitioner has raised the question of vendor's title on the one hand and possession of the suit property by himself on the other. The law lays down that the jurisdiction to decree specific performance is discretionary and the court is not bound to grant such relief merely because it is lawful to do so. This discretion is guided by sound judicial principles. Section 25 of the Specific Relief Act inter alia, lays down that a contract for sale cannot be specifically enforced in favour of a vendor who knowing himself not to have any title to the property has contracted to sell the same. It is, therefore necessary in view of section 25 and the principles laid down in the aforesaid cases that the petitioner should be added as a party so that an effective decree may be passed and the plaintiff may not be driven to further litigation. 

 10. Mr. M.H. Khandker, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party No.1 has submitted that the petitioner cannot be allowed to be added as a party so as to convert the suit for specific performance into a complicated title suit and that it is a general proposition that parties cannot be added so as to alter the nature of the suit. Is support of his submission Mr. Khandker has referred to the case of Abdul Gafur and others Vs. Ali Miah 28 C. W.N. 805. That was a suit for rent and it was held that parties should not be added in a suit for rent so as to transform it into a complex title suit. It was, however, observed that the provision of Order], rule 10, Sub-Rule (2) C.P.C. confers a discretion upon the Court, which must be exercised in view of the special circumstances of the particular litigation, subject, however, to the general proposition as stated above. It further says that a person may be added a party to a suit only in two cases; first, when he ought to have been joined and has not been so joined, or secondly, when without his presence the suit cannot be completely decided. This decision, relied upon, by Mr. Khandker, does not apply in terms to 'the facts of the present case but the observations made therein as referred to above are quite opposite and in line with the principles referred to earlier. The introduction of the petitioner in the suit shall not be for the purpose of obtaining a decree as to title to the property but only for the limited purpose of ascertaining whether the vendor knowing about his absence of title contracted to sell as alleged. 

 11. Secondly, the petitioner's presence is very much necessary because he claims to be in possession of the suit property. If his possession is proved, no decree for possession can be passed against him and the suit for specific performance would fail although a Suit for damages may lie against the vendor. Mr. Khandker referred to two decisions, reported in 5 DLR (Dacca) 39 and 12 DLR (Dacca) 708 and sought to advance a proposition in favour of the co-sharer-vendor that a co-sharer in exclusive possession of a specific portion of ejmali land is entitled to maintain his possession as against other co-sharers such as the petitioner is and the latter's remedy is only by way of a suit for partition.The proposition is not disputed. The question, however, is whether in the facts and circumstances of' the present case the petitioner should be added as a party defendant in the suit brought against his co-sharer. The principles governing addition of party in a suit of the present kind as referred to above have not been disputed by Mr. Khandker nor any contrary decision has been cited before us.
